paper.instructions:
(i) This question paper contains 33 questions. All questions are compulsory.
(ii) Question paper is divided into FIVE sections - Section A, B, C, D and E.
(iii) SECTION A - Question number 1 to 16 are Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ) type questions. Each question carries 1 mark.
(iv) SECTION B - Question number 17 to 21 are Very Short Answer type questions. Each question carries 2 mark.
(v) SECTION C - Question number 22 to 28 are Short Answer type questions. Each question carries 3 mark.
(vi) SECTION D - Question number 29 and 30 are Case-Based questions. Each question carries 4 mark.
(vii) SECTION E - Question number 31 to 33 are Long Answer Type questions. Each question carries 5 mark.
(viii) There is no overall choice given in the question paper. However, an internal choice has been provided in few questions in all the Sections except Section-A.
(ix) Kindly note that there is a separate question paper for Visually Impaired candidates.
(x) Use of calculators NOT allowed.

questions.stem:
(a) (i) Define mutual inductance. Write its SI unit.
(ii) Derive an expression for the mutual inductance of a system of two long coaxial solenoids of same length $l$, having turns $N_1$ and $N_2$ and of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ ($> r_1$)
questions.solution:
(a) (i) Mutual Inductance : It is numerically equal to the magnetic flux linked with one coil (secondary coil) when a unit current flows through the other coil (primary coil).
Unit $\rightarrow$ H or henry
(ii) For I coil, $\phi_1 = M_{12} I_2 \quad ...(1)$
Where $\phi_1$ is the flux through I coil.
Similarly,
$$\phi_1 = (B_2 \cdot A_1)N_1 = \left(\frac{\mu_0 N_2 I_2}{\ell}\right)A_1 N_1 = \frac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 A_1 I_2}{\ell} \quad ...(2)$$
From (1) & (2)
$$M_{12} I_2 = \frac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 A_1 I_2}{\ell}$$
$$\Rightarrow M_{12} = \frac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 A_1}{\ell}$$
questions.or_stem: What are ferromagnetic materials ? Explain ferromagnetism with the help of suitable diagrams, using the concept of magnetic domain.
questions.or_solution:
Ferromagnetism : Ferromagnetic substances are those which gets strongly magnetised when placed in an external magnetic field. They have strong tendency to move from a region of weak magnetic field to strong magnetic field, i.e., they get strongly attracted to a magnet.

The individual atoms (or ions or molecules) in a ferromagnetic material possess a dipole moment as in a paramagnetic material. However, they interact with one another in such a way that they spontaneously align themselves in a common direction over a macroscopic volume called domain. The explanation of this cooperative effect requires quantum mechanics and is beyond the scope of this text book. Each domain has a net magnetisation. Typical domain size is $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ and the domain contains about $10^{11}$ atoms. In the first instant, the magnetisation varies randomly from domain to domain and there is no bulk magnetisation. This is shown in Fig. (a). When we apply an external magnetic field $B_0$, the domains orient themselves in the direction of $B_0$ and simultaneously the domain oriented in the direction of $B_0$ grow in size. This existence of domains and their motion in $B_0$ are not speculations. One may observe this under a microscope after sprinkling a liquid suspension of powdered ferromagnetic substance of samples. This motion of suspension can be observed. Fig. (b) shows the situation when the domains have aligned and amalgamated to form a single 'giant' domain.

Thus, in a ferromagnetic material the field lines are highly concentrated. In non-uniform magnetic field, the sample tends to move towards the region of high field.

questions.stem: Two conducting spherical shells A and B of radii $R$ and $2R$ are kept far apart and charged to the same charge density $\sigma$. They are connected by a wire. Obtain an expression for final potential of shell A.
questions.solution:
$$V_1 = \frac{Kq_1}{R}$$
$$V_2 = \frac{Kq_2}{2R} = \frac{K(4q_1)}{2R} = 2V_1$$
$$V = \frac{C_1 V_1 + C_2 V_2}{C_1 + C_2}$$
$$\because q_1 = \sigma \times 4\pi R^2 \quad \therefore q_2 = \sigma \times 4\pi(2R)^2$$
$$q_2 = 4q_1$$
$$C = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R, \quad C_1 = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R, \quad C_2 = 4\pi\epsilon_0 2R$$
$$C_2 = 2C_1$$
$$V = \frac{C_1 V_1 + 2C_1 2V_1}{C_1 + 2C_1} = \frac{5C_1 V_1}{3C_1} = \frac{5}{3}V_1$$
$$= \frac{5}{3}\frac{K(\sigma \times 4\pi R^2)}{R} = \frac{5}{3} \times \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \times \sigma \times 4\pi R$$
$$V = \frac{5\sigma R}{3\epsilon_0}$$

questions.stem:
Explain the following giving reasons :
(i) 'Electromagnetic waves differ considerably in their mode of interaction with matter'.
(ii) 'Food items to be heated in microwave oven must contain water'.
(iii) 'Welders wear face mask with glasses during welding'.
questions.solution:
(i) The basic difference between various types of EM waves lies in their wavelengths since all of them travel through vacuum with the same speed. Consequently, the waves differ considerably in their mode of interaction with matter. They interact with matter via their electric and magnetic fields which set in oscillation charges present in all matter. The detailed interaction and so the mechanism of absorption, scattering etc., depend on the wavelength of the electromagnetic wave, and the nature of the atoms and molecules in the medium.
(ii) When the temperature of a body rises, the energy of random motion of atoms and molecules increases and the molecules travel or vibrate or rotate with higher energies. The frequency of rotation of water molecules is about $3\ \mathrm{GHz}$. If water receives microwaves of this frequency, its molecules absorb this radiation which is equivalent to heating up water. These molecules share this energy with neighbouring food molecules, heating up the food.
(iii) To protect their eyes from large amount of UV (ultraviolet) produced by welding arcs.

questions.stem:
(a) Differentiate between nuclear fission and fusion.
(b) The fission properties of $_{94}\mathrm{Pu}^{239}$ are very similar to those of $_{92}\mathrm{U}^{235}$. How much energy (in MeV), is released if all the atoms in $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of pure $_{94}\mathrm{Pu}^{239}$ undergo fission? The average energy released per fission is $180\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
questions.solution:
(a) Nuclear fission : Nuclear fission is the phenomenon of splitting of a heavy nucleus (usually $A > 230$) into two or more lighter nuclei.
Ex. $_{92}\mathrm{U}^{235} + {}_{0}\mathrm{n}^{1} \rightarrow {}_{92}\mathrm{U}^{236} \rightarrow {}_{56}\mathrm{Ba}^{141} + {}_{36}\mathrm{Kr}^{92} + 3\,{}_{0}\mathrm{n}^{1} + Q$
Nuclear fusion : The process of combining of two lighter nuclei to form one heavy nucleus is called nuclear fusion.
Ex. $4\,{}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{1} \rightarrow {}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4} + 2\,{}_{1}\mathrm{e}^{0} + 2\nu + 26.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$
Fission is more polluting and lesser amount of energy got released in it compared to fusion.
Nuclear reactor is based on controlled chain reaction.
(b) $\because$ No. of atoms in $239\ \mathrm{g} = 6 \times 10^{23}$
$\therefore$ No. of atoms in $1\ \mathrm{g} = \frac{6 \times 10^{23}}{239}$
Energy from $1\ \mathrm{g} = \frac{6 \times 10^{23}}{239} \times 180\ \mathrm{MeV}$
$= 4.5 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{MeV}$

questions.stem:
A pure semiconductor like Ge or Si, when doped with a small amount of suitable impurity, becomes an extrinsic semiconductor. In thermal equilibrium, the electron and hole concentration in it are related to the concentration of intrinsic charge carriers. A p-type or n-type semiconductor can be converted into a p-n junction by doping it with suitable impurity. Two processes, diffusion and drift take place during formation of a p-n junction. A semiconductor diode is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for the application of an external voltage. A p-n junction diode allows currents to pass only in one direction when it is forward biased. Due to this property, a diode is widely used to rectify alternating voltages, in half-wave or full wave configuration.

(i) When Ge is doped with pentavalent impurity, the energy required to free the weakly bound electron from the dopant is about :-
(A) $0.001\ \mathrm{eV}$
(B) $0.01\ \mathrm{eV}$
(C) $0.72\ \mathrm{eV}$
(D) $1.1\ \mathrm{eV}$
(ii) At a given temperature, the number of intrinsic charge carriers in a semiconductor is $2.0 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. It is doped with pentavalent impurity atoms. As a result, the number of holes in it becomes $8 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. The number of electrons in the semiconductor is :-
(A) $2 \times 10^{24}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$
(B) $4 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$
(C) $1 \times 10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$
(D) $5 \times 10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$
(iii) (a) During the formation of a p-n junction -
(A) electrons diffuse from p-region into n-region and holes diffuse from n-region into p-region
(B) both electrons and holes diffuse from n-region into p-region.
(C) electrons diffuse from n-region into p-region and holes diffuse from p-region into n-region.
(D) both electrons and holes diffuse from p-region into n-region.
OR
(b) Initially during the formation of p-n junction -
(A) diffusion current is large and drift current is small.
(B) diffusion current is small and drift current is large.
(C) both the diffusion and the drift currents are large.
(D) both the diffusion and the drift currents are small.
(iv) An ac voltage $V = 0.5 \sin (100 \pi t)$ volt is applied, in turn, across a half-wave rectifier and a full-wave rectifier. The frequency of the output voltage across them respectively will be :-
(A) $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$
(B) $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $100\ \mathrm{Hz}$
(C) $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$
(D) $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $100\ \mathrm{Hz}$
questions.solution:
(i) (B) $0.01\ \mathrm{eV}$
(ii) (D) $n_e = \frac{4 \times 10^{20} \times 10^{6}}{8 \times 10^{3}} = 5 \times 10^{22}\ \mathrm{/m^{3}}$
(iii) (a) (C) electrons diffuse from n-region into p-region and holes diffuse from p-region into n-region.
OR
(b) (A) diffusion current is large and drift current is small.
(iv) (D) $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $100\ \mathrm{Hz}$

questions.stem:
A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces ; at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula of image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a thin lens, a formula known as lens maker's formula and hence the basic lens formula can be obtained. The focal length (or power) of a lens depends on the radii of its surfaces and the refractive index of its material with respect to the surrounding medium. The refractive index of a material depends on the wavelength of light used. Combination of lenses helps us to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired power and magnification.

(i) A thin converging lens of focal length $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ and a thin diverging lens of focal length $15\ \mathrm{cm}$ are placed coaxially in contact. The power of the combination is :-
(A) $\frac{-5}{6}\ \mathrm{D}$
(B) $\frac{-5}{3}\ \mathrm{D}$
(C) $\frac{4}{3}\ \mathrm{D}$
(D) $\frac{3}{2}\ \mathrm{D}$
(ii) The radii of curvature of two surfaces of a convex lens are $R$ and $2R$. If the focal length of this lens is $\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)R$, the refractive index of the material of the lens is :-
(A) $\frac{5}{3}$
(B) $\frac{4}{3}$
(C) $\frac{3}{2}$
(D) $\frac{7}{5}$
(iii) The focal length of an equiconvex lens :-
(A) increases when the lens is dipped in water.
(B) increases when the wavelength of incident light decreases.
(C) increases with decrease in radius of curvature of its surface.
(D) decreases when the lens is cut into two identical parts along its principal axis.
(iv) (a) A thin convex lens L of focal length $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ and a concave mirror M of focal length $15\ \mathrm{cm}$ are placed coaxially $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart as shown in figure. A beam of light coming parallel to the principal axis is incident on the lens. The final image will be formed at a distance of :-
(A) $10\ \mathrm{cm}$, left of lens
(B) $10\ \mathrm{cm}$, right of lens
(C) $20\ \mathrm{cm}$, left of lens
(D) $20\ \mathrm{cm}$, right of lens
OR
(b) A beam of light coming parallel to the principal axis of a convex lens $L_{1}$ of focal length $16\ \mathrm{cm}$ is incident on it. Another convex lens $L_{2}$ of focal length $12\ \mathrm{cm}$ is placed coaxially at a distance $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ from $L_{1}$. The nature and distance of the final image from $L_{2}$ will be
(A) real, $24\ \mathrm{cm}$
(B) virtual, $12\ \mathrm{cm}$
(C) real, $32\ \mathrm{cm}$
(D) virtual, $18\ \mathrm{cm}$
questions.solution:
(i) (B) $\frac{-5}{3}\ \mathrm{D}$
$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{15}$
$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{3-4}{60} = \frac{-100}{60} \Rightarrow P = \frac{-5}{3}\ \mathrm{D}$
(ii) (C) $\frac{3}{2}$
$\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{2R}\right)$
$\frac{3}{4R} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{2+1}{2R}\right)$
$\frac{1}{2} = (\mu - 1) \Rightarrow \mu = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5$
(iii) (A) Increases when the lens is dipped in water.
(iv) (a) (B) $10\ \mathrm{cm}$, right of lens
OR
(b) (A) real, $24\ \mathrm{cm}$

questions.stem:
(i) A dielectric slab of dielectric constant 'K' and thickness 't' is inserted between plates of a parallel plate capacitor of plate separation d and plate area A. Obtain an expression for its capacitance.
(ii) Two capacitors of different capacitances are connected first (1) in series and then (2) in parallel across a dc source of $100\ \mathrm{V}$. If the total energy stored in the combination in the two cases are $40\ \mathrm{mJ}$ and $250\ \mathrm{mJ}$ respectively, find the capacitance of the capacitors.
questions.solution:
(i) Total potential difference.
$V = V_{slab} + V_{air} = E_{slab} \times t_{slab} + E_{air}\, t_{air}$
$= \frac{\sigma}{K\varepsilon_{0}}\, t + \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}}\,(d - t)$
$V = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}A}\left[\frac{t}{K} + (d + t)\right]$
So, capacitance of PPC.
$C = \frac{Q}{V}$
$C = \frac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{\left[\frac{t}{k} + (d - t)\right]}$

(ii) Consider two capacitors of capacitance $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$.
In series $C_{S} = \frac{C_{1} \cdot C_{2}}{C_{1} + C_{2}}$
$U_{S} = \frac{1}{2} C_{S} V^{2} = 40\ \mathrm{mJ}$ ...(1)
In parallel $C_{P} = C_{1} + C_{2}$
$U_{P} = \frac{1}{2} C_{P} V^{2} = 250\ \mathrm{mJ} \Rightarrow C_{P} = \frac{500\ \mathrm{mJ}}{V^{2}}$ ...(2)
$U_{S} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{C_{1}C_{2}}{C_{1} + C_{2}}\right)V^{2} = 40\ \mathrm{mJ}$
$U_{S} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{C_{1}C_{2}}{500\ \mathrm{mJ}} \times V^{2} \times V^{2} = 40\ \mathrm{mJ}$ $\left(\because C_{1} + C_{2} = \frac{500\ \mathrm{mJ}}{V^{2}}\right)$
$C_{1}C_{2} = \frac{40 \times 10^{-3} \times 500 \times 10^{-3} \times 2}{(10^{2})^{4}} = 500 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{-4} = 5 \times 10^{5}$
$C_{1}C_{2} = 4 \times 10^{-10}$ ...(3)
$(C_{1} - C_{2})^{2} = (5 \times 10^{-5})^{2} - 4(4 \times 10^{-10}) = 9 \times 10^{-10}$
so $C_{1} - C_{2} = 3 \times 10^{5}$ ...(4)
$C_{1} + C_{2} = 5 \times 10^{-5}$
$C_{1} = 4 \times 10^{-5}$
$C_{1} = 40\ \mu\mathrm{F}$
so $C_{2} = 10\ \mu\mathrm{F}$
questions.or_stem:
(i) Using Gauss's law, show that the electric field $\vec{E}$ at a point due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet is given by $\vec{E} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\hat{n}$ where symbols have their usual meanings.
(ii) Electric field $\vec{E}$ in a region is given by $\vec{E} = \left(5x^{2} + 2\right)\hat{i}$ where E is in N/C and x is in meters. A cube of side $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ is placed in the region as shown in figure. Calculate (1) the electric flux through the cube, and (2) the net charge enclosed by the cube.
questions.or_solution:
(i) As shown in figure, considering a cylindrical Gaussian surface of cross section A
Flux through curved surface :
$\phi = \int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s} = \int E\, ds \cos 90^\circ = 0$
At the points on the curved surface, the field vector $\vec{E}$ and area vector $d\vec{s}$ make an angle $90^\circ$ with each other. Therefore, curved surface does not contribute to the flux.
Flux through end caps :
$\phi = \oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s} = \oint E\, ds \cos 0^\circ = EA$
Hence, the total flux through the closed surface is :
$\phi$ = Flux through both end caps + flux through curved surface
or $\phi = EA + EA + 0 = 2EA$ (1)
Now according to Gauss' law for electrostatics
$\phi = q/\varepsilon_{0}$ (2)
Comparing equations (1) and (2), we get
$2EA = q/\varepsilon_{0}$
$E = q/2\varepsilon_{0}A$ (3)
The area of sheet enclosed in the Gaussian cylinder is also A. Therefore, the charge contained in the cylinder, $q = \sigma A$ as $\sigma$ (surface charge density) $= q/A$
Substituting this value of q in equation (3), we get
$E = \frac{\sigma A}{2\varepsilon_{0}A}$
or $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}} \Rightarrow \vec{E} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\hat{n}$
This is the relation for electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge. The field is uniform and does not depend on the distance from the plane sheet of charge.

(ii) $\vec{E} = (5x^{2} + 2)\,\hat{i}\ \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}$
$\phi_{1} = \vec{E}_{1} \cdot \vec{A} = -2 \times 10^{-2}\ \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{m^{2}}$ (at $x = 0$)
$\phi_{2} = \vec{E}_{2} \cdot \vec{A} = -\left[5 \times (0.1)^{2} + 2\right] \times 10^{-2}$ (at $x = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$)
$\phi_{2} = 2.05 \times 10^{-2}\ \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{m^{2}}$
net flux $= \phi_{1} + \phi_{2} = -2 \times 10^{-2} + 2.05 \times 10^{-2} = 0.05 \times 10^{-2} = 5 \times 10^{-4}\ \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{m^{2}}$
$\phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_{0}}$
$q = \varepsilon_{0} \times \phi = 8.80 \times 10^{-12} \times 5 \times 10^{-4}$
$q = 44.25 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{C}$

questions.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram for the formation of the image of an object by a concave mirror. Hence, obtain the mirror equation.
(ii) Why are multi-component lenses used for both the objective and the eyepiece in optical instruments ?
(iii) The magnification of a small object produced by a compound microscope is 200. The focal length of the eyepiece is $2\ \mathrm{cm}$ and the final image is formed at infinity. Find the magnification produced by the objective.
questions.solution:
(i) Relation between u, v and f for concave mirror :
u $\Rightarrow$ distance between pole and object
v $\Rightarrow$ distance between pole and image
f $\Rightarrow$ focal length
In $\Delta A'FB'$ and $\Delta RFQ$
$\angle QFR = \angle A'FB'$ and $\angle A'B'F = \angle RQF = 90^\circ$
$\therefore \Delta A'FB' \sim \Delta RFQ$, so
$\frac{A'B'}{QR} = \frac{FB'}{QF} \Rightarrow \frac{A'B'}{AB} = \frac{FB'}{QF}$ ...(1) {from figure $QR = AB$}
Similarly $\Delta ABC \sim \Delta A'B'C$, hence
$\frac{A'B'}{AB} = \frac{B'C}{BC}$ ...(2)
From eq. (1) and (2)
$\frac{FB'}{QF} = \frac{B'C}{BC}$
Point Q is very close to P. Hence $\Rightarrow QF \approx PF$
$\frac{PB' - PF}{PF} = \frac{PC - PB'}{PB - PC}$
Applying sign convention $PB' = -v$, $PF = -f$, $PC = -2f$ and $PB = -u$
$\frac{-v - (-f)}{-f} = \frac{-2f - (-v)}{u - (-2f)}$
On solving, $uv - uf = vf$
divide by uvf
$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v}$ (This is mirror's equation).
(ii) To reduce aberrations.
(iii) $m = 200$, $f_{e} = 2\ \mathrm{cm}$, $m_{o} = ?$
$v_{e} = \infty$, $u_{e} = f_{e} = 2\ \mathrm{cm}$
$m = m_{o} \times m_{e}$
$m = m_{o} \times \frac{D}{f_{e}}$
$200 = m_{o} \times \frac{25}{2}$
$m_{o} = 16$
questions.or_stem:
(i) Differentiate between a wave front and a ray.
(ii) State Huygen's principle and verify laws of reflection using suitable diagram.
(iii) In Young's double slit experiment, the slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ are $3\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart and the screen is placed $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the slits. It is observed that the fourth bright fringe is at a distance of $5\ \mathrm{mm}$ from the second dark fringe. Find the wavelength of light used.
questions.or_solution:
(i) Ray represents it is the direction of propagation of light energy. While the locus of all the particles of the medium vibrating in the same phase at a given instant is called a wavefront, and ray is $\perp$ to wavefront.
(ii) According to Huygens principle "each point on a wave front acts as a source of new disturbance, called secondary wavelets. These wavelets are spherical and travel with speed of light in that medium".
(iii) $d = 3\ \mathrm{mm}$, $D = 1\ \mathrm{m}$
Position of 4th bright fringe $-$ position of 2nd dark fringe $= 5\ \mathrm{mm}$
$\frac{4\lambda D}{d} - \frac{3\lambda D}{2d} = 5 \times 10^{-3}$
$y_{n} = \frac{n\lambda D}{d}$ (const. int.)
$y_{n}' = (2n - 1)\frac{\lambda D}{2d}$ (Dest. int.)
By solving $\lambda = 6 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m} = 6000\ \mathrm{nm}$

questions.stem:
(i) Mention the factors on which the resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit depends. Plot a graph showing variation of impedance of a series LCR circuit with the frequency of the applied a.c. source.
(ii) With the help of a suitable diagram, explain the working of a step-up transformer.
(iii) Write two causes of energy loss in a real transformer.
questions.solution:
(i) Frequency depends on value of inductance & capacitance.
as $f_{r} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$
(ii) $N_{s} > N_{p}$
Principle: Transformer works on principle of mutual induction, in which an EMF is induced in the secondary coil due to the change in magnetic flux linked with it because of change in current in primary coil.
Working : When alternating current source is connected to the ends of primary coil, the current changes continuously in the primary coil, due to which magnetic flux linked with the secondary coil changes continuously. Therefore, the alternating emf of same frequency is developed across the secondary terminals.
When alternating current flows through the primary coil, an emf is induced in the neighbouring (secondary) coil due to mutual induction.
Induced emf produced in the primary coil is
$E_{P} = -N_{P}\,(d\phi/dt)$ (self induction)
In the secondary coil, it will be
$E_{S} = -N_{S}\,(d\phi/dt)$ (mutual induction)
Hence $\frac{E_{S}}{E_{P}} = \frac{-N_{S}\frac{d\phi}{dt}}{-N_{P}\frac{d\phi}{dt}} = \frac{N_{S}}{N_{P}} \Rightarrow \frac{E_{S}}{E_{P}} = \frac{N_{S}}{N_{P}}$
Let $I_{P}$ and $I_{S}$ be the current in the primary and secondary coil respectively, under ideal condition. For ideal transformer
Output power = Input power
$V_{S}I_{S} = V_{P}I_{P}$
$\frac{V_{S}}{V_{P}} = \frac{I_{P}}{I_{S}}$ $\left\{\frac{V_{S}}{V_{P}} = \frac{N_{S}}{N_{P}}\right\}$
$\frac{N_{S}}{N_{P}} = \frac{I_{P}}{I_{S}}$
(iii) (1) Hysteresis loss : Transformer cores are magnetised and demagnetised repeatedly, so lot of electrical energy is wasted in the form of heat in this process. To reduce this loss cores are made of soft iron, which has small hysteresis loop area.
(2) Eddy current loss : The alternating magnetic flux induces eddy currents in the iron core causes heating. The effect is reduced by laminating the core.
To reduce electrical energy losses in the form of heat energy, power is transmitted at high voltage upto large distances.
questions.or_stem:
(i) With the help of a diagram, briefly explain the construction and working of ac generator.
(ii) An electron is revolving around a proton in an orbit of radius r with a speed v. Obtain expression for magnetic moment associated with the electron.
questions.or_solution:
(i) $B_{1}$ & $B_{2}$ are carbon brushes. $S_{1}$ & $S_{2}$ are slip rings. [1]
Let at any instant (t), the angle between $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{A}$ is $\theta$, then the magnetic flux linked with coil at that instant.
$\phi_{B} = N\left(\vec{B} \cdot \vec{A}\right) = NBA \cos\theta$ [1]
(N = number of turns in the coil, A = area of the coil, $\omega$ = angular velocity of coil)
$\phi_{B} = NBA \cos\omega t$ $\{\because \theta = \omega t\}$
$\frac{d\phi_{B}}{dt} = NBA\omega\,(-\sin\omega t)$
Thus induced emf, $e = -\frac{d\phi_{B}}{dt}$
or $e = NBA\omega \sin\omega t$
$e = e_{0} \sin\omega t$ $\{\because e_{0} = NBA\omega\}$ [1]
(ii) Magnetic moment $\mu = IA = \frac{q}{T} \times \pi r^{2} = \frac{-e}{2\pi r} \times v \times \pi r^{2}$
$\mu = -\frac{evr}{2}$ ... (1)
$\mu = -\frac{e}{2m}\, mvr$ ...(2)
$\vec{\mu} = \frac{-e}{2m}\vec{L}$ ... (3)
$\because mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$
By eq. (2)
$\mu = \frac{-e}{2m} \times \frac{nh}{2\pi}$
$|\mu| = \frac{neh}{4\pi m}$
When $n = 1$, $|\mu| = B_{M}$
$B_{M} = \frac{eh}{4\pi m}$
Where $B_{M}$ = Bohr Magneton.
